forces.title: Digitalisation enhances thermal power plant efficiency and reliability
forces.description: The rapid adoption of digitalisation and AI in thermal power plants (TPPs) is a significant tailwind for coal consumption efficiency. Technologies such as drones for monitoring, predictive analytics for maintenance, and advanced combustion optimization improve operational efficiency, reduce downtime, and enhance plant reliability, ensuring better utilization of coal as a fuel source. This directly contributes to coal power plant fuel security and economic viability.

forces.title: Global thermal coal demand declines due to cleaner energy alternatives
forces.description: Thermal coal demand is projected to decline globally across all scenarios, with cheaper alternatives displacing aging coal power facilities. China alone is expected to account for over 60% of this global reduction by 2040. While coal retains a role in some regions, the overarching trend indicates a diminishing market share for thermal coal, posing a significant long-term headwind for thermal coal mining and sales.

forces.title: Metallurgical coal demand persists for industrial iron and steel production
forces.description: Demand for metallurgical coal, a crucial input for industrial iron and steel production, is expected to persist into the longer term. This segment of coal demand is less affected by the displacement seen in thermal coal, providing a stable and continued market for coking coal suppliers. This persistence helps mitigate the overall decline faced by the broader coal sector.

forces.title: Ferrous scrap increasingly substitutes coking coal in steelmaking
forces.description: The growing adoption of ferrous scrap as a strategic raw material for Indian steelmakers is a direct headwind for coking coal. Scrap reduces steelmakers' dependence on carbon-intensive inputs, cuts emissions, and mitigates exposure to coking coal price volatility. As India aims to increase its scrap utilization (currently 23% vs. 32% global average) to meet decarbonization and production targets, coking coal demand for steel will face structural pressure.

forces.title: Formalization of India's domestic ferrous scrap market drives efficiency
forces.description: Efforts to formalize India's fragmented ferrous scrap market, including establishing certified collection centers, harmonized quality standards, digital traceability, and streamlined integration of various scrap sources, represent a significant structural change. This transformation aims to improve scrap utilization, making it bankable, traceable, and specification-compliant. Such advancements will further enable scrap's role as a reliable input for steelmaking, thereby intensifying the pressure on coking coal demand.

forces.title: Nuclear power capacity expansion competes with thermal coal
forces.description: India's government plans to significantly increase nuclear power capacity from 8,180 MW in FY26 to 22,480 MW by 2031-32, and further to 100 GW by 2047. This expansion of a dispatchable, low-carbon baseload power source directly competes with thermal coal for electricity generation, posing a long-term headwind for coal demand in the power sector. This policy-driven growth aims to meet energy demands and environmental goals.

forces.title: Natural gas sector expansion intensifies competition for coal
forces.description: India's aggressive expansion of its natural gas sector, with plans to increase gas's share in the energy mix from 6.5% to 15% by 2030, presents a headwind for coal. This growth is driven by City Gas Distribution (CGD) networks, LNG stations, and rising industrial and power sector consumption. As natural gas offers a cleaner-burning alternative, its increased availability and consumption will directly compete with coal in various industrial and energy applications.

forces.title: Ambitious renewable energy targets displace thermal coal generation
forces.description: India's target to achieve 500 GW of installed renewable energy capacity by 2030, including 280 GW from solar power, represents a significant headwind for thermal coal. The rapid increase in renewable generation, evidenced by a 22.85% YoY growth in electricity generation from RES (excluding large hydro) in April 2025–February 2026, directly displaces thermal coal in the power grid, reducing overall demand and impacting coal power plant fuel security.

forces.title: Coal India Limited diversifies significantly into renewable energy projects
forces.description: Coal India Limited's (CIL) approval of joint ventures to develop renewable energy projects, with a planned equity investment of Rs. 3,132 crore (US$ 342.39 million) in projects totaling Rs. 20,886 crore (US$ 2.31 billion), marks a critical structural change. This substantial investment signifies CIL's strategic diversification into clean energy, reducing its sole reliance on coal mining. This shift impacts the future growth trajectory and capital allocation within the Coal & Consumable Fuels sub-industry.

forces.title: Economic incentives favor replacing coal plants with renewable sources
forces.description: The expectation that replacing coal plants with renewable sources will save India Rs. 54,000 crore (US$ 8.4 billion) annually due to reduced power costs creates a powerful economic headwind for thermal coal. This financial incentive drives policy and investment towards accelerating renewable energy deployment and decommissioning coal-fired power plants, directly threatening the demand and long-term viability of thermal coal.

forces.title: Robust domestic coal production supports India's energy needs
forces.description: India's domestic coal production surpassing one billion tonnes in FY2024-25, with a 5-year Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 7.5%, demonstrates a strong tailwind for the Coal & Consumable Fuels sub-industry. This high production volume underscores India's continued reliance on domestic supply to fuel both power generation and industrial activity, ensuring a substantial base demand for coal in the medium term, despite decarbonization efforts.

forces.title: India's decarbonization paradox creates uncertainty for coal's future
forces.description: The 'decarbonization paradox' in India, characterized by the simultaneous expansion of clean energy capacity and a growing fossil fuel base (coal), creates a significant key risk. While India pursues ambitious net-zero targets, the country's economic growth continues to drive absolute fossil fuel consumption. This inherent tension between climate ambition and development needs generates uncertainty for coal's long-term trajectory and the sustainability of coal-related investments.

forces.title: Gas with CCUS emerges as low-carbon baseload alternative
forces.description: The development of gas-fired power generation combined with Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) as a "technology-ready solution" represents a significant headwind. This technology offers a low-carbon baseload alternative, particularly for energy-intensive consumers like data centers, and directly competes with thermal coal in the power sector. Expanding globally, it can displace coal and reshape the competitive landscape for reliable power generation.

forces.title: Continued reliance on coal imports signals strong domestic demand
forces.description: India's import of over 243 million tonnes of coal in FY2024-25, in addition to robust domestic production, indicates persistent and strong internal demand for coal. This reliance on imports to bridge the gap between domestic supply and consumption acts as a tailwind, ensuring that overall coal volumes remain high in the market. It underscores the ongoing need for coal to meet the country's energy and industrial requirements.

viewpoints.title: Digitalisation is critical for thermal power plant efficiency and reliability
viewpoints.description: KPMG, through Powerline Magazine, views digitalisation as a critical lever for thermal power plants (TPPs). It is seen as essential for improving operational efficiency, enhancing reliability, and enabling flexible operations within a grid increasingly dominated by renewable energy. Digital interventions, including drones, AI, and predictive analytics, facilitate real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimized fuel management, ultimately reducing operational risks and improving overall plant performance in the Coal & Consumable Fuels sub-industry.

viewpoints.title: Thermal coal demand to decline, coking coal demand to persist globally
viewpoints.description: Bain projects a global decline in thermal coal demand across all scenarios, driven by cheaper alternatives displacing aging coal power facilities. However, thermal coal is expected to maintain a significant role in key regions like India and China, reflecting persistent regional demand. Conversely, demand for metallurgical coal, essential for industrial iron and steel production, is forecast to persist into the longer term, providing a more stable outlook for that specific segment within Coal & Consumable Fuels.

viewpoints.title: Ferrous scrap adoption strategically reduces coking coal dependence for steelmakers
viewpoints.description: EY identifies ferrous scrap as a strategic lever for Indian steelmakers, directly impacting coking coal demand. Increased scrap adoption reduces dependence on coking coal and other fossil fuels, cutting emissions and mitigating logistics volatility. Despite India's current low scrap utilization compared to global averages, policies and digitalization efforts are formalizing the scrap market, implying a future reduction in demand for coking coal as a primary input, posing a cautious outlook for this segment of consumable fuels.

viewpoints.title: Coal India strategically diversifies into clean energy to adapt to transition
viewpoints.description: Coal India Limited (CIL) is strategically aligning with India's clean energy transition by establishing a 'Centre for Sustainable Energy' with IIT Madras. This initiative focuses on developing low-carbon technologies and repurposing coal mines. This move indicates a proactive approach to adapt to evolving energy landscapes, recognizing the need for diversification beyond traditional coal operations, and potentially mitigating long-term risks associated with a declining thermal coal market.

viewpoints.title: Coal remains pivotal in India's energy mix despite decarbonization efforts
viewpoints.description: EY projects coal to remain a major component of India's primary energy mix, likely exceeding 40% by 2050, driven by the nation's economic growth and development needs. This outlook acknowledges India's 'decarbonization paradox,' where ambitious clean energy targets coexist with rising absolute fossil fuel consumption. The continued reliance on coal for power generation and industrial fuel underscores its enduring importance in the short to medium term for the Coal & Consumable Fuels sub-industry.

demand_drivers.description: Coal remains the primary fuel for India's vast thermal power plant fleet, critical for meeting rising electricity demand driven by economic growth and population increase.
Key industries like cement, steel (for process heat), and various manufacturing sectors rely heavily on coal as a cost-effective energy source for their operations.
India's rapid economic expansion and industrial activity directly translate into higher energy demand, which is currently largely met by coal.

pnl_drivers.description: High domestic coal production volumes directly contribute to revenue for coal mining companies like Coal India, impacting profitability.

Significant coal import volumes indicate sustained demand that domestic supply cannot fully meet. Import costs (influenced by global prices and exchange rates) impact overall fuel security costs for end-users.

market_sizing.methodology: India's domestic coal production exceeded one billion tonnes in FY2024-25, alongside over 243 million tonnes of imports, indicating continued strong reliance on coal for power and industry despite clean energy expansion. This reflects how the system fuels power generation and industry.
